name: Social Studies
description: Your community and the whole wide world are waiting for you! In this course you'll discover what makes a community special and meet the helpers who keep us safe and healthy. You'll learn to read maps and keys, find the seven continents and five oceans, and never get lost with north, south, east, and west. Then you'll travel back in time to meet the first Americans, brave explorers, the 13 colonies, and the story of how America became its own country!

You'll also see how government and citizens work together—what leaders do, how laws are made, and why voting matters. Get ready to feel like part of something bigger and to understand the place you call home.

units.title: My Community
units.description: What makes a community? Meet helpers, learn about rules and laws, and compare city, suburb, and country.

lessons.title: What Is a Community?
lessons.description: Learn that a community is a place where people live, work, and play together.

pages.title: Welcome to What Is a Community?

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn what a community is and why it matters. A community is a place where people live, work, and play together. By the end of this lesson, you'll understand how communities are formed and what makes them special!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding what you'll learn will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Who Lives in a Community?
body: A community is made up of all kinds of people — families, neighbors, shop owners, and more. Everyone in a community has a role to play. Some people run businesses, some teach at schools, and others help keep the streets clean.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding who lives in a community? will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of who lives in a community?
body.caption: A visual guide to who lives in a community?.

sections.heading: Working Together
body: People in a community work together to make their neighborhood a great place to live. They share parks, libraries, and roads. When neighbors help each other, the whole community becomes stronger and happier.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding working together will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Sharing and Caring
body: Communities are special because people care about one another. Neighbors might bring food when someone is sick or wave hello on the street. Small acts of kindness make a community feel like home.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding sharing and caring will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of sharing and caring
body.caption: A visual guide to sharing and caring.

sections.heading: Celebrating Together
body: Communities often celebrate holidays, festivals, and events together. These celebrations bring people closer and help everyone feel like they belong. Think about events you enjoy in your own community!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding celebrating together will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Remember This
body: A community is a place where people live, work, and play together. People in a community share spaces and help each other. Communities are made stronger when everyone does their part!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding remember this will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

options: A place where only animals live
A place where people live, work, and play together
A game you play at recess
question.answer: A place where people live, work, and play together

lessons.title: Community Helpers
lessons.description: Meet firefighters, doctors, teachers, and other helpers.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will meet the amazing people who help keep your community running. From firefighters to teachers, community helpers have important jobs that keep everyone safe, healthy, and happy. Let's find out what they do!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding what you'll learn will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Firefighters and Police Officers
body: Firefighters rush to put out fires and rescue people in emergencies. Police officers protect the community by making sure everyone follows the law. Both of these helpers are brave people who work hard to keep us safe every day.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding firefighters and police officers will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of firefighters and police officers
body.caption: A visual guide to firefighters and police officers.

sections.heading: Doctors and Nurses
body: When you feel sick or get hurt, doctors and nurses are there to help you feel better. They work in hospitals and clinics. Doctors figure out what's wrong, and nurses take care of you while you heal.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding doctors and nurses will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Teachers and Librarians
body: Teachers help you learn new things every day at school. They plan lessons, answer your questions, and help you grow. Librarians help you find great books and learn how to research topics you're curious about.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding teachers and librarians will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of teachers and librarians
body.caption: A visual guide to teachers and librarians.

sections.heading: Mail Carriers and Sanitation Workers
body: Mail carriers deliver letters and packages to your home, rain or shine. Sanitation workers pick up trash and recycling so your community stays clean. Without these helpers, our neighborhoods would not run smoothly.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding mail carriers and sanitation workers will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: So Many Helpers!
body: Your community is full of people who help every day. Firefighters, doctors, teachers, mail carriers, and many more all work together. Next time you see a community helper, thank them for what they do!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding so many helpers! will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

question.text: Which community helper puts out fires?

lessons.title: Rules and Laws
lessons.description: Understand why communities need rules to stay safe.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will discover why communities need rules and laws. Rules help people get along, stay safe, and treat each other fairly. By the end, you'll understand the difference between rules and laws and why both are important.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding what you'll learn will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: What Are Rules?
body: Rules are instructions that tell us how to behave. At home, your parents might have rules like "no running inside." At school, your teacher might say "raise your hand before speaking." Rules help everyone know what to expect.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding what are rules? will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of what are rules?
body.caption: A visual guide to what are rules?.

sections.heading: Keeping Everyone Safe
body: Imagine a playground with no rules — kids could push, cut in line, and break things. Rules keep everyone safe and make sure things are fair. When we follow rules, everyone gets a turn and nobody gets hurt.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding keeping everyone safe will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

pages.title: Rules and Laws in Our Community

sections.heading: What Are Laws?
body: Laws are like rules, but they are made by the government and apply to everyone in a community, city, or country. For example, traffic laws tell drivers to stop at red lights. Laws help keep the whole community safe and organized.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding what are laws? will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of what are laws?
body.caption: A visual guide to what are laws?.

sections.heading: What Happens When Rules Are Broken?
body: When someone breaks a rule at school, they might lose recess time. When someone breaks a law, there are bigger consequences, like paying a fine. Consequences help people remember to follow the rules next time.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding what happens when rules are broken? will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Rules Keep Us Together
body: Rules and laws are important because they keep us safe and help us treat each other fairly. Rules can be found at home, at school, and in your community. Following the rules makes life better for everyone!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding rules keep us together will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

question.text: Why do communities have rules and laws?
options: To keep people safe and treat each other fairly
To give teachers something to talk about
To make sure nobody has fun
question.answer: To keep people safe and treat each other fairly

lessons.title: Urban, Suburban, and Rural
lessons.description: Compare life in a city, suburb, and the countryside.

pages.title: Welcome to Urban, Suburban, and Rural

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will explore three types of communities: urban, suburban, and rural. Each type is different in exciting ways. By the end, you'll be able to tell them apart and describe what makes each one unique!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding what you'll learn will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Urban Communities — The City
body: An urban community is a big city with lots of people, tall buildings, and busy streets. Cities have subways, buses, and many stores and restaurants. People in cities often live in apartments and can walk to many places.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding urban communities — the city will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of urban communities — the city
body.caption: A visual guide to urban communities — the city.

sections.heading: Suburban Communities — Near the City
body: A suburban community is found just outside a city. Suburbs have neighborhoods with houses, yards, and quieter streets. Many families live in suburbs because they have good schools and parks, but they can still drive to the city for work.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding suburban communities — near the city will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Life in the Countryside
body: A rural community is out in the countryside, far from big cities. There is lots of open land, farms, and forests. People in rural areas might grow crops or raise animals. Homes are spread far apart, and nature is all around.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding life in the countryside will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of life in the countryside
body.caption: A visual guide to life in the countryside.

sections.heading: Comparing All Three
body: Urban areas are crowded and busy, suburban areas are in between, and rural areas are quiet and spacious. Each type of community has its own special things to offer. No matter where you live, your community is important!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding comparing all three will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Every Community Is Special
body: Urban means city, suburban means near a city, and rural means the countryside. All three types of communities have homes, schools, and people who care about each other. Think about which type of community you live in!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding every community is special will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

options: A big city with tall buildings
A neighborhood just outside a city
A countryside area with farms and open land
question.answer: A countryside area with farms and open land

units.title: Maps & Geography
units.description: Read maps and keys, find the continents and oceans, and learn north, south, east, and west!

lessons.title: What Is a Map?
lessons.description: Learn that maps show us places from above.

pages.title: Welcome to What Is a Map?

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn what a map is and how it helps us find places. A map is a drawing that shows what a place looks like from above. By the end, you'll know how to look at a simple map and understand what it shows!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding what you'll learn will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: A Bird's-Eye View
body: Imagine you are a bird flying high in the sky. Looking down, you would see the tops of buildings, roads, and parks. A map shows places the same way — from above! This is called a bird's-eye view.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding a bird's-eye view will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of a bird's-eye view
body.caption: A visual guide to a bird's-eye view.

sections.heading: Why We Use Maps
body: Maps help us find where things are and how to get from one place to another. You might use a map to find your classroom, your favorite park, or even a whole country. Maps are one of the most useful tools people have ever made.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding why we use maps will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Maps of Small and Big Places
body: Some maps show small areas, like your school or neighborhood. Other maps show big areas, like a state, a country, or even the whole world! The size of the area on the map depends on what you need to find.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding maps of small and big places will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of maps of small and big places
body.caption: A visual guide to maps of small and big places.

sections.heading: Physical Maps and Political Maps
body: A physical map shows natural features like mountains, rivers, and lakes. A political map shows borders between countries and states. Both types of maps give us different and important information about a place.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding physical maps and political maps will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Maps Are Everywhere
body: Maps are drawings that show places from a bird's-eye view. They help us find locations and plan how to get there. There are many kinds of maps, each with a special purpose!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding maps are everywhere will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

options: What a place looks like from above
question.answer: What a place looks like from above

lessons.title: Map Symbols and Keys
lessons.description: Read a map legend to understand what the symbols mean.

pages.title: Welcome to Map Symbols and Keys

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn how to read map symbols and use a map key. Maps use small pictures and shapes called symbols to stand for real things. A map key, or legend, tells you what each symbol means. Let's become map readers!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding what you'll learn will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Symbols Stand for Real Things
body: A map symbol is a small picture or shape that represents something real. For example, a tiny tree might stand for a forest, a blue line might mean a river, and a small square could be a building. Symbols make maps easier to read.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding symbols stand for real things will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of symbols stand for real things
body.caption: A visual guide to symbols stand for real things.

sections.heading: Common Map Symbols
body: Many maps use similar symbols. A star often marks a capital city, a dotted line can show a trail, and a triangle might represent a mountain. Once you learn the common symbols, you can read many different maps!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding common map symbols will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: What Is a Map Key?
body: A map key, also called a legend, is a small box on the map that explains what each symbol means. It's like a secret code! You look at a symbol on the map, then check the key to find out what it represents.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding what is a map key? will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of what is a map key?
body.caption: A visual guide to what is a map key?.

sections.heading: Practice Reading a Key
body: Next time you see a map, look for the map key first. Find each symbol in the key, then look for it on the map. This is the best way to understand what the map is showing you. Practice makes perfect!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding practice reading a key will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Be a Map Detective
body: Map symbols are small pictures or shapes that stand for real things. A map key tells you what each symbol means. Always check the key first when you look at a new map!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding be a map detective will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

question.text: What does a map key (legend) do?
options: It locks the map so nobody can open it
It explains what the symbols on the map mean
It shows you how old the map is
It tells you who drew the map
question.answer: It explains what the symbols on the map mean

lessons.title: Continents and Oceans
lessons.description: Name the 7 continents and 5 oceans of the world.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn the names of the 7 continents and 5 oceans on Earth. Continents are huge areas of land, and oceans are vast bodies of salt water. By the end, you'll be able to name them all!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding what you'll learn will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Land All Around the World
body: The seven continents are Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, and South America. Asia is the biggest continent, and Australia is the smallest. Each continent has its own countries, animals, and cultures.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding land all around the world will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of land all around the world
body.caption: A visual guide to land all around the world.

sections.heading: Where Do We Live?
body: We live on the continent of North America! North America includes the United States, Canada, and Mexico, plus many other countries. It stretches from the icy Arctic in the north to warm Central America in the south.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding where do we live? will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Water Covers Most of Earth
body: Did you know that more than 70% of Earth is covered in water? The five oceans are the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, and Arctic. The Pacific Ocean is the largest and deepest ocean on the planet.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding water covers most of earth will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of water covers most of earth
body.caption: A visual guide to water covers most of earth.

sections.heading: Oceans Connect Us
body: Oceans separate the continents, but they also connect people by allowing ships to travel between them. Oceans are home to millions of plants and animals, from tiny plankton to giant whales. Taking care of our oceans is very important.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding oceans connect us will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Our Big, Beautiful World
body: Earth has 7 continents and 5 oceans. The continents are huge landmasses, and the oceans are vast stretches of water. Together, they make up everything on our planet's surface!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding our big, beautiful world will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

question.text: How many continents are there on Earth?

lessons.title: Cardinal Directions
lessons.description: Learn north, south, east, and west with a compass rose.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn the four cardinal directions: north, south, east, and west. You'll also discover what a compass rose is and how it helps you read maps. By the end, you'll be able to give and follow directions like a pro!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding what you'll learn will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: The Four Main Directions
body: The four cardinal directions are north, south, east, and west. North points toward the top of most maps. South is the opposite of north, at the bottom. East is to the right, and west is to the left.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding the four main directions will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of the four main directions
body.caption: A visual guide to the four main directions.

sections.heading: A Trick to Remember
body: Here's a fun way to remember the order! Start at the top and go clockwise: North, East, South, West. You can use the phrase "Never Eat Soggy Waffles" to help you remember. Each word starts with the right letter!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding a trick to remember will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: What Is a Compass Rose?
body: A compass rose is a special symbol found on maps that shows the four directions. It looks like a star with points labeled N, S, E, and W. Whenever you're reading a map, look for the compass rose to figure out which way is which.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding what is a compass rose? will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of what is a compass rose?
body.caption: A visual guide to what is a compass rose?.

sections.heading: Using Directions in Real Life
body: You can use cardinal directions every day! The sun rises in the east and sets in the west. If someone says "the park is north of the school," you know to go up on the map. Knowing directions helps you explore the world.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding using directions in real life will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Find Your Way
body: The four cardinal directions are north, south, east, and west. A compass rose on a map shows you these directions. Remember: Never Eat Soggy Waffles!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding find your way will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

question.text: What tool on a map shows north, south, east, and west?

units.title: American History Basics
units.description: The first Americans, explorers, the 13 colonies, and the American Revolution—the story of how America began.

lessons.title: The First Americans
lessons.description: Learn about Native American peoples and their way of life.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn about the Native American peoples who were the first to live in North America. They built amazing communities, created beautiful art, and lived closely with nature. Let's explore their incredible way of life!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding what you'll learn will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: The Very First People
body: Long before cities and cars, Native American peoples lived across North America. They were here for thousands of years before European explorers arrived. There were hundreds of different groups, each with their own language, traditions, and culture.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding the very first people will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of the very first people
body.caption: A visual guide to the very first people.

sections.heading: Living with the Land
body: Native Americans had a deep connection to nature. They hunted animals, fished in rivers, and grew crops like corn, beans, and squash. They used natural resources wisely and respected the land that provided for them.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding living with the land will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Different Groups, Different Lives
body: Native Americans lived in many different environments, from forests to deserts to plains. Groups in the Southwest built homes from clay called adobe. Plains peoples followed buffalo herds. Northwest Coast peoples built large wooden homes near the ocean.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding different groups, different lives will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of different groups, different lives
body.caption: A visual guide to different groups, different lives.

sections.heading: Art, Stories, and Traditions
body: Native Americans created beautiful pottery, woven baskets, and beadwork. They told stories to teach lessons and pass down their history. Many of these rich traditions are still celebrated and honored by Native American communities today.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding art, stories, and traditions will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Honoring the First Americans
body: Native American peoples were the first to live in North America. They had diverse cultures, spoke many languages, and lived closely with nature. Their traditions and contributions are an important part of American history.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding honoring the first americans will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

question.text: What crops did many Native Americans grow?

lessons.title: Explorers
lessons.description: Discover the explorers who traveled to the Americas.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will discover the European explorers who sailed across the ocean to reach the Americas. You'll learn why they came, what they found, and how their voyages changed the world forever.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding what you'll learn will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Looking for New Lands
body: Hundreds of years ago, European countries wanted to find new trade routes and riches. Explorers set sail across the Atlantic Ocean hoping to discover new lands. They were brave, but their journeys were long and dangerous.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding looking for new lands will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of looking for new lands
body.caption: A visual guide to looking for new lands.

sections.heading: Christopher Columbus
body: In 1492, Christopher Columbus sailed from Spain with three ships. He was trying to reach Asia but landed in the Caribbean islands instead. His voyage opened the door for more Europeans to travel to the Americas.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding christopher columbus will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Other Famous Explorers
body: After Columbus, many more explorers came. John Cabot explored the coast of North America for England. Hernán Cortés traveled to Mexico, and Jacques Cartier explored Canada for France. Each explorer claimed land for their home country.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding other famous explorers will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of other famous explorers
body.caption: A visual guide to other famous explorers.

sections.heading: The Impact on Native Peoples
body: When explorers arrived, Native American peoples were already living on the land. The arrival of Europeans brought big changes, including new diseases and conflicts. It is important to remember that exploration affected Native peoples in many difficult ways.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding the impact on native peoples will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: A World Changed Forever
body: European explorers like Columbus, Cabot, and Cartier sailed to the Americas looking for new lands and wealth. Their voyages changed the world, but they also had a serious impact on the Native American peoples who already lived there.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding a world changed forever will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

question.text: In what year did Christopher Columbus first sail to the Americas?

lessons.title: The 13 Colonies
lessons.description: Learn how the first 13 colonies were formed.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn about the 13 colonies that became the first states of the United States. You'll find out where they were, who lived there, and what daily life was like for the colonists.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding what you'll learn will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Settling in a New Land
body: Starting in the early 1600s, people from England and other European countries sailed to North America to start new lives. They built settlements called colonies along the east coast. Jamestown, Virginia, founded in 1607, was one of the first.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding settling in a new land will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of settling in a new land
body.caption: A visual guide to settling in a new land.

sections.heading: Why People Came
body: People moved to the colonies for many reasons. Some wanted religious freedom, like the Pilgrims who settled in Plymouth. Others came to find wealth or to own land. Life in the colonies was hard, but the settlers worked together to survive.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding why people came will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Three Regions
body: The 13 colonies were split into three regions: New England, the Middle Colonies, and the Southern Colonies. New England had cold winters and rocky soil. The Middle Colonies grew lots of grain. The Southern Colonies had large farms called plantations.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding three regions will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of three regions
body.caption: A visual guide to three regions.

sections.heading: Daily Life for Colonists
body: Children in the colonies helped with chores like feeding animals and fetching water. They went to small schoolhouses or learned at home. Families grew their own food, made their own clothes, and worked very hard every day.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding daily life for colonists will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: From Colonies to Country
body: The 13 colonies were settled along the east coast of North America by people from Europe. They came for freedom, land, and new opportunities. These colonies would one day become the United States of America!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding from colonies to country will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

question.text: How many colonies later became the first states of the United States?

lessons.title: The American Revolution
lessons.description: Find out how America became its own country.

video.title: Kurzgesagt – The Birth of a Nation

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn how the 13 colonies fought for their freedom from Britain and became the United States of America. You'll discover what the colonists were unhappy about and how brave people stood up for liberty.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding what you'll learn will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Taxes Without a Say
body: Britain ruled the 13 colonies and made them pay taxes on things like tea and paper. The colonists were angry because they had no voice in the British government. They said this was unfair and called it "taxation without representation."
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding taxes without a say will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of taxes without a say
body.caption: A visual guide to taxes without a say.

sections.heading: Standing Up for Freedom
body: Colonists began to protest. The Boston Tea Party was a famous event where colonists dumped tea into the harbor to show they were upset. Leaders like Samuel Adams and Patrick Henry spoke out, saying the colonies deserved to be free.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding standing up for freedom will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: The Declaration of Independence
body: On July 4, 1776, the colonies declared their independence from Britain. Thomas Jefferson wrote the Declaration of Independence, which said that all people have the right to life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. This was a bold and brave step.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding the declaration of independence will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of the declaration of independence
body.caption: A visual guide to the declaration of independence.

sections.heading: Winning the War
body: The Revolutionary War lasted about eight years. George Washington led the American army through many tough battles. With help from France, the Americans finally won their independence in 1783. The United States of America was born!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding winning the war will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Freedom and Independence
body: The colonists were upset about unfair taxes and no say in government. They declared independence on July 4, 1776, and fought the Revolutionary War. With courage and teamwork, they created a brand-new country.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding freedom and independence will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

question.text: Who wrote the Declaration of Independence?

units.title: Government & Citizens
units.description: What is government? Learn about the President, how laws are made, and why voting matters.

lessons.title: What Is Government?
lessons.description: Learn why we need leaders to make decisions for everyone.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn what a government is and why every community needs one. A government is a group of people who make rules and decisions for everyone. By the end, you'll understand how government helps keep things fair and organized.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding what you'll learn will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Making Decisions for Everyone
body: Imagine if everyone made their own rules — it would be chaos! A government makes decisions so that everyone follows the same rules. It builds roads, runs schools, and keeps people safe. Government helps a community work together smoothly.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding making decisions for everyone will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of making decisions for everyone
body.caption: A visual guide to making decisions for everyone.

sections.heading: Different Levels of Government
body: There are three main levels of government in the United States: local, state, and national. Your city or town has a local government. Your state has a state government. And the whole country has a national government in Washington, D.C.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding different levels of government will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Services for Everyone
body: The government provides many services we use every day. It pays for public schools, fire departments, and libraries. It also builds parks and keeps our drinking water clean. Without government, these important services might not exist.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding services for everyone will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of services for everyone
body.caption: A visual guide to services for everyone.

sections.heading: Leaders We Choose
body: In the United States, the people get to choose their leaders by voting. This is called a democracy. Citizens vote for mayors, governors, and the President. Voting gives everyone a voice in how the government is run.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding leaders we choose will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Government Is for Everyone
body: Government is a group of people who make rules and provide services for a community. The United States has local, state, and national governments. In a democracy, people vote to choose their leaders.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding government is for everyone will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

question.text: What are the three levels of government in the United States?

lessons.title: The President
lessons.description: Find out what the President does and where they live.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn about the President of the United States. You'll find out what the President does, where they live, and why the President is such an important leader. Let's take a peek inside the White House!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding what you'll learn will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Leader of the Country
body: The President is the leader of the United States and the head of the national government. They help make important decisions, sign new laws, and meet with leaders from other countries. It is one of the biggest and most important jobs in the world.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding leader of the country will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of leader of the country
body.caption: A visual guide to leader of the country.

sections.heading: Commander in Chief
body: The President is also the commander in chief of the military, which means they are in charge of the Army, Navy, Air Force, and other branches. The President works to keep the country safe and to solve problems peacefully whenever possible.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding commander in chief will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Where the President Lives
body: The President lives and works in the White House, a big white building in Washington, D.C. The White House has 132 rooms, including an oval-shaped office where the President works. It has been the home of every President since John Adams.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding where the president lives will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of where the president lives
body.caption: A visual guide to where the president lives.

sections.heading: How Someone Becomes President
body: To become President, a person must be at least 35 years old and born in the United States. Citizens vote in an election every four years to choose the President. A President can serve a maximum of two terms, which is eight years total.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding how someone becomes president will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: A Very Important Job
body: The President leads the country, signs laws, and lives in the White House. Citizens vote to choose the President every four years. The President works hard to keep the nation safe and running smoothly.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding a very important job will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

question.text: Where does the President of the United States live and work?

lessons.title: Making Laws
lessons.description: See how an idea becomes a law that everyone follows.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn how a new law is made in the United States. It all starts with an idea! You'll follow that idea through Congress and all the way to the President's desk. By the end, you'll know how an idea becomes a law.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding what you'll learn will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: It Starts with an Idea
body: Anyone can have an idea for a new law — even you! But to become a real law, the idea needs to be written down as a bill. A member of Congress writes the bill and shares it with other members so they can read and discuss it.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding it starts with an idea will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of it starts with an idea
body.caption: A visual guide to it starts with an idea.

sections.heading: Congress Discusses and Votes
body: Congress is made up of two groups: the Senate and the House of Representatives. Both groups talk about the bill, suggest changes, and then vote. If more than half of both groups vote yes, the bill moves on to the next step.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding congress discusses and votes will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: The President Signs the Bill
body: After Congress approves a bill, it goes to the President. If the President agrees with it, they sign it, and it becomes a law! If the President disagrees, they can veto the bill, which means they say no. Congress can try again with more votes.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding the president signs the bill will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of the president signs the bill
body.caption: A visual guide to the president signs the bill.

sections.heading: Why Laws Matter
body: Laws protect people and keep communities running smoothly. Laws say you must wear a seatbelt, go to school, and not steal. Every law started as a simple idea that someone thought would make life better for everyone.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding why laws matter will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Ideas Become Laws
body: A law starts as an idea, gets written as a bill, is voted on by Congress, and is signed by the President. This process makes sure that new laws are carefully discussed and agreed upon before they take effect.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding ideas become laws will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

question.text: What happens after Congress approves a bill?
options: It goes to the President to be signed
It goes back to the person who wrote it
question.answer: It goes to the President to be signed

lessons.title: Voting
lessons.description: Understand how people choose their leaders by voting.

sections.heading: What You'll Learn
body: In this lesson, you will learn about voting and why it is one of the most important things citizens can do. Voting is how people choose their leaders and have a say in their government. By the end, you'll understand how voting works!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding what you'll learn will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Making Your Voice Heard
body: Voting means making a choice. When you vote, you pick the person or idea you think is best. In the United States, citizens vote to choose leaders like the President, governors, and mayors. Every single vote matters!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding making your voice heard will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of making your voice heard
body.caption: A visual guide to making your voice heard.

sections.heading: Voting Is a Right
body: In the United States, citizens who are 18 years or older can vote. It wasn't always this way — long ago, only some people were allowed to vote. Over time, brave people fought to make sure that all citizens could have a voice.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding voting is a right will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Election Day
body: On Election Day, people go to a polling place to cast their vote. They can also vote by mail. Voters mark their choice on a ballot, which is a special form. After everyone votes, the ballots are counted and the winner is announced.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding election day will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

body.alt: Illustration of election day
body.caption: A visual guide to election day.

sections.heading: Voting in School
body: You don't have to wait until you're 18 to practice voting! At school, you might vote for class president or pick a book for the class to read. Voting in school teaches you how to make fair choices and respect other people's opinions.
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding voting in school will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

sections.heading: Every Vote Counts
body: Voting is how citizens choose their leaders and have a say in government. On Election Day, people cast their ballots at polling places or by mail. Voting is a right and a responsibility — every vote counts!
Let's explore this idea a bit further. Understanding every vote counts will help you in many areas. The more you practice, the more confident you'll become!

question.text: How old must a United States citizen be to vote?
